titre: Adam Smith's Invisible Hand, a Metaphor Turned Doctrine
accroche: Smith wrote “invisible hand” only three times in more than a million words: never as the key to his system.
contenu_vulgarise:
Anyone who has taken an economics course has heard of Adam Smith's “invisible hand”: the mechanism by which the pursuit of individual interest would produce, without intending to, the common good. It is the most-quoted phrase in all of economic thought, and yet, in the more than a million words of Smith's that survive, written between 1744 and 1790, the expression “invisible hand” appears only three times.

## Three Occurrences, Three Minor Contexts

The first, in 1759, is found in *The Theory of Moral Sentiments* (*La Théorie des sentiments moraux*, Part IV, Chapter I): a selfish landowner, without meaning to, distributes the fruits of his lands almost as if they had been divided equally among all those who work them, “led by an invisible hand.” The second, in 1776, is found in *The Wealth of Nations* (*La Richesse des nations*, Book IV, Chapter II): a merchant who prefers to invest at home rather than abroad, out of sheer caution, unknowingly favors national industry, “led by an invisible hand to promote an end that was no part of his intention.” The third occurrence is not economic at all: in an early text on the history of astronomy, Smith uses the image to mock superstitious explanations, the invisible hand of Jupiter, which the ancients invoked for lack of understanding natural phenomena.

In none of the three cases does Smith designate a general principle. It is a figure of speech, used once per work, never taken up again, never theorized as such. The historian of economic thought Gavin Kennedy showed this in detail in 2009: nothing in Smith's corpus suggests that he saw it as anything other than a handy image, inherited, moreover, from a long English literary tradition that predates him.

## A Doctrine Built After the Fact

What changed the size of the metaphor was not Smith but the 20th century. In 1948, the economist Paul Samuelson made it, in his textbook *Economics* (the best-selling one in the discipline's history), the central illustration of equilibrium through markets. The expression then begins to circulate independently of the text that produced it, and becomes the name of a doctrine that Smith never formulated as such: that the sum of individual selfishnesses, left to itself, optimizes collective wealth.

The shift goes beyond a biographical anecdote. Smith, in *The Wealth of Nations*, devotes most of his argument to describing the abuses of merchants, the need for public rules, and his distrust of guilds: far more than to celebrating a spontaneous order that he mentions only once in 900 pages. A foundational text is rarely read for itself: it is read through what generations of readers have chosen to take from it, sometimes to the point of inverting it. The invisible hand became the bedrock of economic liberalism at the precise moment it stopped being read in context.

It is the economist Paul Samuelson who, in his 1948 textbook Economics, makes it the key to equilibrium through markets: two centuries after Smith wrote it in passing.

quiz.question: Why does the central place of the “invisible hand” in economics textbooks surprise an attentive reader of Adam Smith?
choix: Because Smith invented it to describe only how the labor market works
Because Smith uses it only three times, in minor passages, without ever presenting it as a theory
Because Smith disowned the idea in a late edition of his work
Because the expression appears only in a manuscript left unpublished during Smith's lifetime
quiz.explication: Smith uses the metaphor only three times, in minor contexts, one of them not economic at all; it is Paul Samuelson who, in 1948, makes it the key to his textbook: Smith neither conceived it for the labor market nor disowned it, and the text was indeed published in his lifetime.
